- External audit gives an opinion on the financial statements; internal audit tests whether the controls behind them work.
- Independence comes from the reporting line: internal audit reports to the board or owners, not to the people it reviews.
- A useful engagement starts from a risk assessment, not a fixed checklist.
- Every finding should name an owner, a deadline and how the fix will be verified.

Most owners first meet the word audit through their external auditor: a firm that arrives after year-end, asks for confirmations and schedules, and signs an opinion on the financial statements. So when someone proposes internal audit, the natural assumption is that it is the same exercise, done more often, by someone closer to home. It is not, and the difference decides whether the money spent on it returns anything.

#### What is internal audit?

The Institute of Internal Auditors, which sets the global standards for the profession, describes internal auditing as independent and objective assurance and advice that helps an organisation protect and create value. In practice that means a systematic, disciplined look at three things: how the business identifies and manages risk, whether its controls work as designed, and whether governance gives the board and owners an accurate picture. The output is not an opinion on the numbers. It is a set of findings and recommendations about the system that produces them.

#### How is it different from an external audit?

- Purpose: the external auditor expresses an opinion on whether the financial statements are fairly presented; internal audit evaluates whether risk, control and governance processes are effective.
- Audience: the external opinion is for shareholders, lenders, tax authorities and other outside users; internal audit reports to the board, the audit committee or the owners.
- Timing: the external audit looks back at a closed year; internal audit works through the year and looks at what is happening now and what could go wrong next.
- Scope: the external auditor is bound by the financial statements; internal audit can review procurement, inventory, payroll, system access, compliance, or anything the risk assessment points to.
- Standards: external auditors work under the International Standards on Auditing; internal auditors follow the IIA’s Global Internal Audit Standards.

The two are complementary. A good internal audit function gives the external auditor a stronger control environment to rely on and a documented evidence trail, which usually shortens the year-end work. It does not replace the external audit, and it should never be sold as if it does.

#### Where does independence come from?

An internal auditor who reports to the finance manager cannot credibly report on the finance manager’s controls. Independence is a matter of reporting line: the function, whether in-house or outsourced, reports its findings to the board, an audit committee, or in an owner-managed company directly to the owners. Management responds to the findings and owns the fixes. The auditor does not design the controls it later tests, and does not run the processes it reviews.

#### What does a small or mid-sized company actually get?

A company without an audit committee or a dedicated team does not need a large department. It needs a structured programme sized to its risks. When MFT runs internal audit for an owner-managed business, the engagement usually delivers the following.

- A risk assessment that ranks the business processes by what could go wrong and how much it would matter, so the work starts where the exposure is.
- An annual audit plan agreed with the owners, covering the high-risk processes first: typically purchasing and payments, sales and receivables, inventory, payroll and system access.
- Testing of the controls in those processes, including segregation of duties, approval limits, reconciliations and the audit trail in the ERP.
- A written report per review, with each finding tied to its evidence, the risk, the root cause, a recommendation, an owner and a target date.
- Follow-up: a later check that the agreed actions were implemented and actually work, not only that someone said they were done.

#### What makes a finding useful?

A finding that says “controls over payments should be strengthened” is not a finding. A useful one states what was tested, what was found, why it matters, and what would fix it. For example: vendor bank details can be changed by the same user who releases payments, and nobody reviews the changes, so a fraudulent change could go unnoticed; restrict the change to a separate role and review a change log monthly. An anomaly is reported as an anomaly, with its evidence. Whether it is an error, a weakness or something worse is established by investigation, not assumed in the report.

> External audit tells you whether last year’s numbers were fair. Internal audit tells you whether next year’s will be.

#### When is the right time to start?

The usual triggers are growth that has outpaced the finance team, a new ERP going live, a second branch or a second country, preparing for investors or a bank facility, or an owner who no longer sees every payment personally. Each of these moves decisions away from the people who used to check them by eye. Internal audit puts a structured check in place of that personal oversight, before a surprise forces the question.

Q: Is internal audit mandatory for private companies?
A: Generally not, although requirements depend on the country, the sector and whether the company is listed or regulated, so check what applies to you. Most private companies adopt internal audit voluntarily because owners, lenders or investors want assurance over controls.

Q: Can internal audit be outsourced?
A: Yes. Many small and mid-sized companies outsource or co-source internal audit to a specialist firm. Independence still depends on the reporting line: the provider reports to the board or owners, and management remains responsible for the controls.

Q: How often should internal audit report?
A: Most programmes report after each review and give the board or owners a periodic summary, often quarterly, of findings and the status of agreed actions. The frequency should follow the risk assessment rather than a fixed calendar.

### Segregation of duties in Odoo: who should never hold both keys
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/segregation-of-duties-odoo/
Published: 2026-09-22

Segregation of duties means no single person controls every stage of a transaction: authorising it, recording it, holding the asset and reconciling the result. In Odoo it is enforced by assigning users to access groups that separate incompatible tasks and by adding approval steps. Where the team is too small, independent review of changes and reconciliations compensates.

- Separate four functions: authorising, recording, custody of assets and reconciliation.
- Map the conflicts by process before assigning Odoo access groups, not after.
- Approvals and lock dates add control where roles cannot be split.
- Small teams compensate with independent, documented review of changes and reconciliations.

In our reviews, the control weaknesses that matter most are rarely sophisticated. They come down to one person being able to do two things that should have been done by two people: add a supplier and pay it, or receive cash and record the receipt. Segregation of duties is one of the oldest internal controls there is, and in an ERP it is also one of the easiest to undo with a single change in the user settings.

#### What is segregation of duties?

The principle is that no single person should control every stage of a transaction. Control frameworks split a transaction into four functions: authorising it, recording it, having custody of the asset involved, and reconciling the records to reality. When one person holds two of those functions, they can both create an error and hide it. The aim is not distrust of any individual. It is a design in which a mistake, or a deliberate misstatement, has to pass through a second pair of hands.

#### Which pairs of duties conflict?

- Creating or changing a vendor, including its bank account, and approving or releasing payments to vendors.
- Raising a purchase order and receiving the goods against it, or approving the vendor bill for the same order.
- Creating customers and setting credit limits, and approving sales on credit or issuing credit notes.
- Receiving cash or customer payments, and posting the receipts or reconciling the bank account.
- Posting manual journal entries, and approving them or changing the lock dates that protect closed periods.
- Administering user access in the system, and processing financial transactions in it.
- Adjusting inventory quantities, and counting or valuing the same stock.

#### How do you implement it in Odoo?

Odoo controls what a user can do through access groups assigned per application. In Accounting the levels run from invoicing-only access up to full accounting and administrator rights; Purchase, Sales and Inventory each have their own user and administrator levels. The exact group names and what each one allows vary by version and edition, which is why we confirm the version before we design the matrix. The practical sequence is the same on every implementation.

- Start from the process, not the system: list who does what in purchasing, sales, treasury, inventory and the close, and mark the conflicting pairs.
- Translate the result into a role matrix, then into Odoo access groups, giving each user the lowest level that lets them do their job.
- Add approval steps where one role must check another: Purchase offers a two-step order approval above an amount you set, and further approvals on payments or entries can be added with Odoo’s approval features, depending on edition.
- Protect closed periods with lock dates, and restrict who can change them.
- Remove administrator rights from anyone who processes transactions, and keep a separate, rarely used administrator account.
- Review the user list and group assignments at least quarterly; access drifts every time someone covers for a colleague on leave.

This is part of how MFT designs an Odoo implementation: the access matrix is signed off by the finance lead before users are created, so the system starts with the separation built in instead of having it retrofitted after the first audit.

#### What if the team is too small to split duties?

A finance team of two cannot separate seven pairs of duties. That does not make the principle irrelevant. It means compensating controls: checks performed by someone outside the transaction, usually the owner or general manager, that would detect what segregation would have prevented.

- The owner approves every new vendor and every change to vendor bank details, from a report of changes to vendor records.
- Bank statements reach the owner directly, and the owner reviews and signs the monthly reconciliation.
- A monthly list of manual journal entries, credit notes and inventory adjustments is reviewed by someone who did not post them.
- Payments above a set amount need a second approver, even if that person sits outside finance.

> Segregation of duties is not about trusting people less. It is about not asking anyone to be the only control.

#### How do you know it is working?

Test it. Export the users and their groups from Odoo and compare them with the approved matrix. Select vendor changes and check who made them and who approved them. Look for anyone who posted and approved the same entry. An internal audit review of access is short when the design is sound, and it is the only way to know the design survived the last year of staff changes.

Q: What is an example of segregation of duties?
A: A common example is that the person who creates a vendor or changes its bank details is not the person who approves or releases payments to that vendor. Another is that the person who receives customer cash does not reconcile the bank account.

Q: Can Odoo enforce segregation of duties?
A: Yes, mainly through access groups per application, approval steps such as purchase order approval above a set amount, and lock dates on closed periods. The available groups and approval features vary by version and edition, so the design should be checked against your installation.

Q: What are compensating controls?
A: They are checks performed by someone independent of the transaction, such as an owner reviewing bank reconciliations or vendor changes, that detect what segregation of duties would otherwise have prevented. They are used when the team is too small to separate conflicting duties.

### Three-way match: the purchase control that stops paying for what never arrived
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/three-way-match-purchase-controls/
Published: 2026-09-24

A three-way match compares the purchase order, the goods receipt and the vendor bill before a payment is approved. Quantities and prices on the bill must agree with what was ordered and what was actually received, within agreed tolerances. Differences are held for review instead of being paid, so the company pays only for goods it ordered and received.

- Match three documents: what was ordered, what was received, and what was billed.
- Tolerances must be written, small, and approved by someone outside purchasing.
- In Odoo, billing on received quantities ties each bill to a validated receipt.
- Partial deliveries, returns and price changes are where the control is really tested.

Ask a finance team how it knows a vendor bill is right and the usual answer is that purchasing confirmed it. That is a two-way check at best: the bill agrees with what someone remembers ordering. The three-way match adds the piece that matters most, evidence that the goods or services actually arrived, and it does so before the payment rather than after.

#### What is a three-way match?

Three documents are compared line by line before a bill is approved for payment:

- The purchase order: what the company authorised, at what price, from which vendor.
- The goods receipt: what the warehouse or the requester confirms was physically received, and in what quantity.
- The vendor bill: what the supplier is asking to be paid for.

If the bill agrees with the order on price and with the receipt on quantity, it can proceed. If it does not, the difference is held and investigated. A two-way match, order against bill, is common for services where there is no physical receipt; even then, a confirmation from the requester that the service was delivered plays the part of the receipt.

#### What tolerances are reasonable?

Exact agreement on every line is rarely practical: rounding, freight, small currency differences and agreed price adjustments all create noise. A tolerance is the difference the company accepts without investigation. There is no standard figure. It should reflect the value of typical purchases and the company’s materiality, and it should be:

- Written in the purchasing policy, separately for quantity and for price.
- Small enough that repeated differences cannot add up to something material over a year.
- Approved by finance, not set by the purchasing team whose bills it applies to.
- Reviewed: a monthly list of bills accepted within tolerance shows whether one vendor is consistently using the full allowance.

#### How does Odoo support it?

Odoo links the three documents natively. A vendor bill can be created from the purchase order, and each bill line keeps a reference to its order line. The product’s bill control setting decides what can be billed: on ordered quantities, the bill can be raised as soon as the order is confirmed; on received quantities, only what has been validated on a receipt can be billed. For stocked goods we set received quantities as the default, which turns the receipt into a hard condition rather than a reminder.

Depending on the version, the Purchase settings also include a three-way matching option that marks each bill according to whether it should be paid, based on the order and the receipts. Price tolerances are not a standard setting, so where a client needs one we enforce the rule through the approval workflow or a small, documented customisation, and confirm the behaviour on the client’s version during testing.

#### What about partial deliveries, returns and price changes?

- Partial deliveries: with billing on received quantities, the vendor can only be billed for what arrived; the balance stays open on the order until the rest is received or the line is closed.
- Returns: a return to the vendor reduces the received quantity, so goods already billed need a vendor credit note, and the return is not closed until that credit note is matched.
- Over-deliveries: goods received above the ordered quantity are approved as a change to the order, or returned, before they are billed.
- Price variance: a bill above the order price is either corrected by the vendor or approved as an order change by someone with authority; it is not quietly accepted by the clerk entering the bill.
- Services and expenses without a receipt: a requester confirmation, recorded against the order, takes the place of the receipt.

Where inventory is valued automatically, the match also reaches the balance sheet. The receipt values the stock at the order price, and a bill at a different price creates a difference that has to be treated according to the costing method. Leaving those differences unreviewed is how inventory valuation drifts away from what was actually paid.

> A bill without a receipt is a request for payment. A bill with one is evidence.

#### How do you test the control?

In an MFT internal audit review we take the bills paid in a period and check, for a risk-based selection, that each one traces to an approved order and a validated receipt, and that differences outside tolerance were approved by someone with authority. We also look for the workarounds: bills recorded without an order, orders created after the bill date, and receipts validated by the person who approved the order. Each is a place where the control was bypassed, and each is visible in the ledger.

Q: What is the difference between a two-way and a three-way match?
A: A two-way match compares the purchase order with the vendor bill. A three-way match adds the goods receipt, so the company confirms that what is billed was actually received before it pays.

Q: Does Odoo support three-way matching?
A: Yes. Odoo links vendor bills to purchase order lines, and setting a product’s bill control to received quantities limits billing to what has been received. Some versions also offer a three-way matching option in the Purchase settings, so confirm the behaviour on your version.

Q: What tolerance should a three-way match allow?
A: There is no standard figure. The tolerance should be small, written in the purchasing policy separately for quantity and price, approved by finance, and reviewed so that repeated differences cannot add up to a material amount.

### Bank reconciliation is a control, not a chore
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/bank-reconciliation-controls/
Published: 2026-09-26

A bank reconciliation is a control because it proves that every movement on the bank statement is recorded in the ledger and every recorded payment actually went through the bank. To work as a control it is done at least monthly, with reconciling items explained and aged, no unexplained difference carried forward, and review by someone who makes no payments.

- Reconcile every account at least monthly, and active accounts weekly.
- Every reconciling item needs an explanation, an owner and an age.
- An unexplained difference is a finding, not a balancing figure.
- The reviewer must not be the person who creates or releases payments.

In many companies the bank reconciliation is the last task of the close, done quickly by whoever has time, with a small difference posted to a suspense account so that the numbers agree. That is the reconciliation as a chore. Treated as a control, the same exercise is the most direct evidence a company has that its cash records are complete and real.

#### Why is bank reconciliation a control?

The bank statement is evidence produced by a third party. Comparing it with the ledger tests two things at once: that every movement on the statement is recorded, which catches unrecorded payments, charges and receipts; and that every payment and receipt in the ledger actually went through the bank, which catches entries that never happened. Few other controls give independent evidence so cheaply.

#### How often should you reconcile?

At least monthly, for every bank account, including dormant accounts and accounts in foreign currency. For operating accounts with frequent movements, weekly is better, and where statements arrive in Odoo every day, daily matching is realistic. The reason is practical: an error found within a week is easy to trace, because the people involved remember the transaction. One found three months later is an investigation.

#### What counts as a reconciling item?

A reconciling item is a legitimate timing difference between the bank and the books, with a known cause and an expected clearing date:

- Outstanding payments: cheques issued or transfers recorded but not yet cleared by the bank.
- Deposits in transit: receipts recorded in the books but not yet credited on the statement.
- Bank charges, interest and fees on the statement that have not yet been recorded.
- Errors by the bank or in the ledger that have been identified and are being corrected.

Each item should have a description, an owner and an age. Items older than a period set in the close procedure, for example thirty days, are escalated: a cheque that has not cleared for months may be lost, cancelled or misused, and a deposit that never arrives is a receivable, not cash.

#### What do you do with an unexplained difference?

Nothing that makes it disappear. An unexplained difference means the reconciliation is not finished, however small the amount. Posting it to a suspense or rounding account hides the very thing the control exists to find, and a small difference can be the visible part of a larger pattern. The difference stays open, is investigated, and is reported to the reviewer with what has been done so far.

> A reconciliation that always balances on the last day, with a small adjustment, has not been reconciled. It has been closed.

#### How does Odoo help?

Odoo imports bank statements from files or, depending on the edition and the bank, through a direct bank feed, and presents each statement line for matching against open invoices, bills and payments. Reconciliation models automate the routine: a rule can match lines to open invoices by reference or partner, or propose a counterpart entry for recurring items such as bank charges, and it can either suggest the match or apply it automatically. Automation belongs only on items that are genuinely routine, and the rules themselves need review, because a badly written model reconciles the wrong things silently.

Lock dates matter here too. Once a period is reconciled and reviewed, locking it prevents back-dated entries from changing a balance that has already been agreed to the bank. When MFT runs an Odoo implementation, the statement import, the reconciliation models and the lock-date procedure are configured and tested with the finance team before the first close.

#### Who should review it?

Someone who does not create or release payments, and who is senior enough to ask questions. In a small company that is usually the owner or general manager. The review is evidenced: the reviewer agrees the closing balance to the statement, reads the list of reconciling items and their ages, asks about anything old or unusual, and signs and dates the reconciliation. Without that step, the reconciliation tells the company only what the preparer chose to show.

Q: How often should bank accounts be reconciled?
A: At least monthly for every account, including dormant and foreign currency accounts. Active operating accounts benefit from weekly or even daily matching, because recent differences are much easier to trace.

Q: What are reconciliation models in Odoo?
A: They are rules that help match bank statement lines, for example to open invoices by reference or partner, or that propose a counterpart entry for recurring items such as bank charges. They can suggest a match for review or apply it automatically, so they should be configured and reviewed with care.

Q: Who should review the bank reconciliation?
A: Someone who does not create or release payments, often the owner, general manager or finance manager. The reviewer agrees the balances, questions old or unusual reconciling items, and signs and dates the reconciliation.

### Virtual CFO or full-time CFO: how to tell which one you need
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/virtual-cfo-vs-full-time-cfo/
Published: 2026-09-28

A Virtual CFO makes sense when a company needs senior finance judgement on planning, cash, reporting and controls, but not every day, typically a growing or owner-managed business with a bookkeeper or small team. A full-time CFO is the better choice when significant finance decisions arise daily, the team needs an on-site leader, or investors and lenders expect one.

- Decide on the amount of senior judgement needed, not the job title.
- A Virtual CFO works on a fixed cadence with defined deliverables.
- Daily decisions, a larger team or investor requirements point to a full-time hire.
- Neither model works without reliable books and a disciplined close.

Owners usually ask this question when something has started to slip: the bank asks for a forecast nobody can produce, a new branch opens without a budget, or the monthly numbers arrive too late to change anything. The instinct is to hire a CFO. Sometimes that is right. Often what the business needs first is a CFO’s judgement for a few days a month, applied to a finance function that is not yet ready for a full-time leader.

#### What does a Virtual CFO actually do?

A Virtual CFO is a senior finance professional, or a small team, who performs the CFO role part-time and usually remotely, under an engagement with a defined scope. The work sits above bookkeeping and below the board: turning the ledger into decisions. A typical scope includes:

- A monthly management pack: profit and loss, balance sheet, cash flow and the few KPIs the owners actually manage by, with commentary on what moved and why.
- Cash management: a rolling cash forecast, a working capital review and early warning of tight weeks or covenant pressure.
- Budgeting and forecasting, and the variance review that keeps a budget useful after the first month.
- Close discipline: a calendar, reconciliations and review, so the numbers are reliable and on time.
- Controls and governance: approval limits, segregation of duties and the reporting the owners or board need.
- Support on decisions and with counterparties: pricing, investment cases, banks, investors and auditors.

#### What cadence should you expect?

The engagement runs on a rhythm, not on request. A common pattern is a weekly cash check, a monthly close review and management meeting, and a quarterly session on the forecast, the budget and the risks ahead. Between those points the Virtual CFO is reachable for decisions that cannot wait. If the arrangement is only activated when something goes wrong, it is advisory work, not a CFO function.

#### When does a Virtual CFO make sense?

- The company has a bookkeeper or a small accounting team that records transactions well, but nobody who interprets them for the owners.
- Finance decisions of consequence come up monthly, not daily.
- The business is preparing for something specific, such as a bank facility, a new market or an ERP change, and needs senior input for a defined period.
- The owners want the discipline of monthly reporting and forecasting before committing to a permanent senior hire.

#### When should you hire a full-time CFO?

- Significant finance decisions arise every day: pricing, treasury, contracts, credit.
- The finance team has grown to the point where it needs a leader on site to direct, train and review its work.
- The company is raising capital, managing several entities or preparing for a listing, and investors or lenders expect a dedicated executive.
- The role needs to sit permanently in the leadership team and own outcomes beyond finance.

The two are not exclusive. Many companies use a Virtual CFO to build the reporting, the forecast and the controls, then hire a full-time CFO into a function that already works, with the Virtual CFO helping to define the role and hand over.

> A CFO is not a job title. It is a quantity of judgement per week. Buy the quantity you need.

#### What are the red flags?

- No defined deliverables: if the engagement letter does not list what arrives each month, nothing reliably will.
- Reports built outside the ledger: spreadsheets that cannot be traced back to the accounting system are opinions, not management information.
- A Virtual CFO who also posts the entries and approves the payments, which removes the independent review the role should provide.
- Forecasts without variance review: a forecast nobody compares with actuals is a document, not a tool.
- On the hiring side, recruiting a CFO before the books are reliable, which turns a strategic hire into a clean-up project.

At MFT the Virtual CFO service starts with the ledger: the books are reviewed and the close is stabilised before the first management pack is issued, because every decision in the role depends on numbers the owners can trust.

Q: What is a Virtual CFO?
A: A Virtual CFO is a senior finance professional or team who performs the CFO role part-time and usually remotely, under an engagement with a defined scope, cadence and deliverables.

Q: Is a Virtual CFO the same as an outsourced accountant?
A: No. An outsourced accountant records transactions and prepares the books and filings. A Virtual CFO interprets those numbers, runs forecasting and management reporting, strengthens controls and supports the owners’ decisions.

Q: When should a company hire a full-time CFO?
A: Usually when significant finance decisions arise daily, the finance team needs an on-site leader, or investors and lenders expect a dedicated finance executive. Many companies make the hire after a Virtual CFO has built reliable reporting and controls.

### How to build a 13-week cash flow forecast from your ledger
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/thirteen-week-cash-flow-forecast/
Published: 2026-09-30

A 13-week cash flow forecast projects cash receipts and payments week by week for the next quarter using the direct method. It starts from the reconciled bank balance, builds receipts from open receivables and expected sales, and payments from payables, payroll, tax and debt service. It is rolled forward every week and compared with actual results.

- Start from the reconciled bank balance, not from profit.
- Use the direct method: actual receipts and payments, week by week.
- Roll the forecast every week, dropping the past week and adding a new one.
- Compare forecast with actual weekly; the variances show where the assumptions are wrong.

Profit and cash rarely move together in the short term. A profitable month can end with less cash than it began, because customers paid late, stock was bought ahead of a season, or a tax payment fell due. The 13-week cash flow forecast exists to answer one question the profit and loss account cannot: will we have enough cash in each of the next thirteen weeks, and if not, in which week does the problem start?

#### Why thirteen weeks?

Thirteen weeks is a quarter. It is long enough to see a shortfall coming while there is still time to act, by chasing collections, rescheduling payments or drawing on a facility, and short enough that most of the numbers come from documents that already exist: open invoices, open bills, purchase orders, payroll and loan schedules. Beyond a quarter a forecast leans more on assumptions; within it, it can be built largely from the ledger.

#### What is the direct method?

The direct method forecasts actual cash in and cash out by category, rather than starting from profit and adjusting for non-cash items as the indirect method does. For a short-term forecast it is the right choice, because the people managing cash think in receipts and payments, and because each line can be traced to its source and checked against what actually happened.

#### How do you build it from the ledger?

- Opening balance: the bank balances reconciled to the statements, for every account the company can actually use.
- Customer receipts: open receivables from the aged balance, each placed in the week it is realistically expected to be paid, based on that customer’s actual payment behaviour rather than the contractual due date.
- New sales: expected collections from sales not yet invoiced, from confirmed orders or the pipeline, kept on a separate line so their uncertainty stays visible.
- Supplier payments: open payables and committed purchase orders, scheduled by agreed terms and the company’s payment runs.
- Payroll and recurring costs: salaries, rent, utilities and subscriptions, in the weeks they actually leave the account.
- Tax and statutory payments: VAT, withholding, social insurance and other obligations, on their filing calendar.
- Financing: loan repayments, interest, facility drawdowns and any owner funding or distributions.
- Closing balance per week, compared with the minimum cash the business needs to operate safely.

In Odoo most of these inputs already exist: the aged receivable and payable reports, open purchase orders, and journal items with due dates. The forecast itself usually lives in a spreadsheet or a planning tool fed from those reports, but every line should trace to the ledger or to a named, written assumption.

#### How does the weekly roll work?

Every week the past week drops off and a new thirteenth week is added. The opening balance is replaced by the actual reconciled balance, open items are refreshed from the ledger, and the assumptions for the remaining weeks are revisited. The roll should take hours, not days. If it takes longer, the inputs are not coming cleanly from the system.

#### Why does variance review matter?

A forecast is only as good as the last time it was checked. Each week, compare what was forecast for the week just ended with what actually happened, line by line. Large variances have an explanation: a customer who pays later than assumed, a supplier paid early, a cost nobody listed. Fix the assumption, not just the number. Over several weeks this review is what turns a spreadsheet into a reliable tool, and it shows the owners which parts of the forecast deserve confidence.

> The point of a cash forecast is not to be right. It is to be wrong early enough to do something about it.

#### Who should own it?

The forecast belongs to finance, but its inputs come from sales, purchasing and operations, and the decisions it prompts belong to the owners or management. In the companies where MFT acts as Virtual CFO, the 13-week forecast is reviewed in a short weekly cash meeting: the closing balance per week, the lowest point in the quarter, the variances from last week, and the actions agreed to protect the tight weeks.

Q: What is a 13-week cash flow forecast?
A: It is a week-by-week projection of cash receipts and payments over the next thirteen weeks, built with the direct method and updated every week. It shows the expected cash balance at the end of each week and highlights when a shortfall could occur.

Q: Should a 13-week forecast use the direct or the indirect method?
A: The direct method is usually preferred, because it projects actual receipts and payments that can be traced to invoices, bills and schedules. The indirect method, which starts from profit, suits longer-term planning better.

Q: How often should a 13-week cash flow forecast be updated?
A: Weekly. Each week the past week is replaced with actuals, a new week is added at the end, and the forecast is compared with actual results to improve the assumptions.

### Odoo 20 for finance teams: what changes, what to ignore, what to test
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/odoo-20-whats-new-for-finance-teams/
Published: 2026-10-06

According to the Odoo 20 release notes, the finance changes that matter are in the bank and payables: bank entries must originate from bank transactions, bills can be paid through bank payment initiation where bank and country allow, and duplicate bills get red or yellow warnings. An AI assistant follows. Re-test ETA and ZATCA e-invoicing after upgrading.

- Odoo 20 was released on 24 September 2026; Odoo 17.0 reaches the planned end of standard support the same month.
- The bank, payables and valuation changes alter controls, not just screens, so they need testing.
- AI features run on IAP credits bought separately, and AI agents are Enterprise-only.
- No Odoo 20 specific ETA or ZATCA changes are verified; re-test e-invoicing in a sandbox anyway.

Odoo 20 was released on 24 September 2026 at Odoo Experience in Brussels, with one version number for Community and Enterprise. For a finance team in Cairo or Riyadh, the more important changes are quieter: how bank entries are created, how bills are paid, how duplicates are caught and how inventory valuation is closed. This is a reading of the Odoo 20 release notes from the finance side: what changes, what can wait, and what to test before you move.

#### Does the release date matter if we are not upgrading yet?

It matters because of support, not features. Odoo supports each major version for three years. According to Odoo’s published plan, standard support for 17.0 ends in September 2026, for 18.0 in September 2027 and for 19.0 in September 2028, which places Odoo 20 at roughly September 2029. If you run 17.0, the question is no longer whether to plan an upgrade but which version to land on. Odoo’s upgrade service can take an Enterprise database across several versions in one request, for example from 17 to 20, but skipping versions raises the testing burden, because every change in between arrives at once.

#### What changes in accounting and the bank?

The most consequential change, according to the release notes, is that all journal entries affecting bank accounts must originate from bank transactions. A manual entry straight to the bank account, the usual cause of a bank balance that no longer agrees with the statement, is no longer the normal path. Around it sit several smaller improvements:

- Refined statement validation feedback to help find and fix balance inconsistencies.
- A bank reconciliation summary report listing reconciled and unreconciled transactions as at the period end date.
- Matching rules that find an open invoice or bill fitting a transaction and reconcile it.
- Analytic distribution on a write-off created during reconciliation.
- Exchange gains and losses consolidated into a single line per invoice, expandable to show the calculation.
- Depreciation that accepts rates and decimal numbers, and intercompany vendor bills auto-matched with synchronized purchase orders.

#### What changes in payables?

Three things. First, bills can be paid from Odoo: select one or several, pay, and confirm with the bank, individually or in batch, through payment initiation (PISP). Availability depends on your bank and country, so confirm it with your bank before you plan around it. Second, invoices and bills get duplicate detection with two levels: red for a highly likely duplicate to correct, yellow for a potential duplicate to investigate before posting, with protection against double payments. Third, bill lines can be predicted from bill history, which speeds entry but also repeats yesterday’s coding mistakes if nobody reviews them.

#### What changes in inventory valuation?

Under perpetual valuation, accrual entries affecting inventory valuation can be made from the inventory valuation closing report and post directly to the inventory valuation account, rather than through the stock variation account. The release notes also list a retroactive COGS update when a cost changes after delivery, landed costs assignable to individual products of a transfer, inventory at a past date, a stock aging report, and the ability to manage stock on hand and valuation without the Inventory app. Each changes how a balance sheet or gross profit figure is produced, so each belongs in your close review.

#### What does the AI assistant do for accounting?

According to the release notes, you can ask the accounting AI assistant about receivables, gross profit or cash flow and get figures drawn from the reports, and it can review suspected bank reconciliation errors and return recommendations. AI features consume IAP credits bought separately from user licences and billed per request. Treat its answers as a fast way to find the right report, and its recommendations as proposals that a person checks against the ledger.

#### What about ETA and ZATCA e-invoicing?

We have not verified any Odoo 20 specific change for Egypt’s ETA e-invoicing or Saudi ZATCA. The localization modules you rely on today still exist, but an upgrade touches the data and code underneath them. After any upgrade, re-test e-invoicing end to end in a sandbox or pre-production environment before production invoices flow.

#### What can a finance team safely ignore for now?

Anything that does not change how a balance is produced or approved can wait for a second phase: presentation changes such as the consolidated exchange difference line, purchasing helpers such as vendor quality ratings and suggested reordering rules, and AI agents until you have decided who governs them.

#### What should you test before you upgrade?

- Any process that posted manual entries to bank accounts, since those entries must now come from bank transactions.
- The bank reconciliation summary report at a month end you have already closed, compared with your own reconciliation.
- Duplicate warnings on a sample of known duplicates and known legitimate repeats.
- Payment initiation with your actual bank, if it is offered for your country, and who is allowed to use it.
- The valuation closing report and COGS on a product whose cost changed after delivery.
- ETA or ZATCA e-invoicing in a sandbox or pre-production environment.

> An upgrade is a change in how your numbers are produced. Test it like one.

When we run an Odoo upgrade for a client, these tests are part of acceptance, run on a copy of the client’s own closed periods, before anyone is asked to sign off.

Q: When was Odoo 20 released?
A: Odoo 20 was released on 24 September 2026 at Odoo Experience in Brussels, with one version number for Community and Enterprise.

Q: How long will Odoo 20 be supported?
A: Odoo supports each major version for three years, which places standard support for Odoo 20 at roughly September 2029. Odoo 17.0 reaches its planned end of standard support in September 2026.

Q: Does Odoo 20 change Egyptian ETA or Saudi ZATCA e-invoicing?
A: No Odoo 20 specific change for ETA or ZATCA is verified. Re-test e-invoicing in a sandbox or pre-production environment after any upgrade, before production invoices are issued.

### Odoo 20 AI agents in finance: useful, billable, and in need of an approver
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/odoo-20-ai-agents-finance-controls/
Published: 2026-10-05

According to the Odoo 20 release notes, AI agents are Enterprise-only records with instructions, skills, knowledge sources and triggers. They can create and update records, run in automated and scheduled actions, and every run is logged. Each request consumes IAP credits. Govern them like a new team member: the agent drafts, a named person approves.

- AI agents are part of Odoo 20 Enterprise, not Community.
- Every request consumes IAP credits, including requests fired by scheduled triggers.
- An agent that can create or update records needs an approver and segregation of duties.
- Keep and review the run logs as audit evidence, not as a debugging aid.

Until now, AI in most ERP systems answered questions. According to the Odoo 20 release notes, AI agents in Odoo 20 go further: they can create and update records and run inside automated and scheduled actions, not only in a chat window. For a finance team that is a real capability and a real control question at the same time. An agent that posts or edits records on a schedule is doing work that, done by a person, would sit inside your approval matrix.

#### What is an AI agent in Odoo 20?

The release notes describe an agent as a record with instructions, reusable skills, knowledge sources and triggers wired to automation rules. Every run is logged. Agents can also connect to outside assistants through MCP. In finance terms, an agent is a standing instruction with the ability to act: it wakes on a trigger, reads what its knowledge sources allow, and changes records within the rights it has been given.

#### What can agents do for finance today?

The release notes name a few finance uses directly. The accounting AI assistant answers questions about receivables, gross profit or cash flow with figures from the reports, and can review suspected bank reconciliation errors and return recommendations. In purchasing, an agent points out vendors worth renegotiating with, and a vendor quality rating is built from past orders. Beyond these, what an agent does depends on how you configure it, which is exactly why configuration is a finance decision and not only an IT one.

#### Who can use them, and what do they cost?

AI agents are part of Odoo 20 Enterprise, not Community. AI features consume IAP credits, bought separately from user licences and billed per request. That includes requests fired by scheduled triggers: a trigger that runs every hour consumes credits every hour, whether or not there was anything useful to do. A cost that grows with a schedule rather than with use is easy to miss in the budget and easy to fix once someone owns it.

- Name an owner for the IAP credit balance and review consumption monthly, by agent.
- Set trigger frequency to the business need: a daily review does not need an hourly trigger.
- Disable agents that no longer have a clear purpose instead of letting them run quietly.

#### How should finance govern an agent that can change records?

The same way it governs a person with the same rights. The fact that the actor is software does not remove the need for authorisation; it removes the excuse that somebody looked.

- The agent drafts. Anything that affects the ledger, a payment or master data stays in draft until a person reviews it.
- A named person approves. Not a role mailbox and not the agent’s owner by default, but a specific approver with authority for that type and size of item.
- Segregation of duties applies. The person who configures an agent’s instructions should not be the only person who approves its output.
- Rights are minimal. Give the agent access to the records it needs and no more, and review those rights when its instructions change.
- Logs are kept. Every run is logged in Odoo; decide how long you keep them and who reviews them, and treat them as audit evidence.

#### What should internal audit look at?

Start with an inventory: which agents exist, what triggers them, what records they can create or update, and who owns each one. Then sample the run logs against the records changed, and check that every ledger-affecting change has an approval by someone other than the agent’s configurer. Check external connections through MCP separately, because they move data beyond the walls of the database. Finally, compare IAP credit consumption with the agents that should be running; unexplained consumption is often the first sign of a forgotten trigger.

> An agent with write access and no approver is not automation. It is an unreviewed journal entry with a schedule.

#### How does this compare with MFT’s own approach?

It is the rule we built MFT Intelligence on, and the subject of our earlier article, Agents draft. People approve. Our agents prepare findings, correcting entries and adjustments; named, registered approvers sign them according to materiality; and corrections are made as reversals, never deletions. Odoo 20 agents can be governed the same way. The tool provides triggers and logs. The approval design is yours to set, before the first agent goes live, not after the first surprise.

If you are evaluating Odoo 20 agents, write down for each one its purpose, its trigger, its rights, its approver and its expected credit use. If you cannot fill in the approver, the agent is not ready.

Q: Are Odoo 20 AI agents available in Community?
A: No. According to the Odoo 20 release notes, AI agents are part of Odoo 20 Enterprise.

Q: How are Odoo AI agents billed?
A: AI features consume IAP credits bought separately from user licences, billed per request, including requests fired by scheduled triggers. A trigger that runs hourly consumes credits hourly.

Q: Can an Odoo 20 agent post accounting entries without approval?
A: Agents can create and update records within the rights they are given. Whether ledger changes need approval is a control you design: keep agent output in draft and require a named approver.

### Odoo 20 bank reconciliation and bill payments: the new rules and the controls they need
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/odoo-20-bank-reconciliation-and-bill-payments/
Published: 2026-10-04

According to the Odoo 20 release notes, every journal entry affecting a bank account must originate from a bank transaction, a summary report shows reconciled and unreconciled items at period end, and bills can be paid through payment initiation where bank and country allow. Pair these with approval before payment, few payment initiators and a reviewed duplicate queue.

- Journal entries affecting bank accounts must originate from bank transactions.
- The reconciliation summary report gives period-end evidence of reconciled and unreconciled items.
- Paying bills via PISP depends on bank and country, and moves payment release into Odoo.
- Red duplicate warnings need correction; yellow ones need investigation before posting.

Bank reconciliation and supplier payments are where most of the cash controls of a company live. According to the Odoo 20 release notes, both change in this version. Some of the changes close gaps we have seen for years. Others move a control from the bank portal into Odoo, which means the control has to move with it.

#### Why must bank entries now originate from bank transactions?

The release notes state that all journal entries impacting bank accounts must originate from bank transactions, to prevent manual entries that break bank consistency. In practice, the classic reconciliation problem is a manual journal entry posted straight to the bank account: a bank charge, a transfer, a correction. The ledger moves, the statement does not, and the difference sits in the reconciliation until someone explains it. Under the new rule, the bank transaction comes first and the accounting follows it.

Finance teams that relied on manual bank entries for transfers between accounts, opening balances or corrections should map those cases before upgrading and decide how each will now be recorded. The release notes also mention refined statement validation feedback to help find and fix balance inconsistencies.

#### What does the reconciliation summary report give you?

A bank reconciliation summary report shows reconciled and unreconciled transactions as at the period end date. That is the document an auditor asks for at every close: what was reconciled, what remained open, and as of when. Make it part of the month-end file, signed by the preparer and a reviewer, and investigate unreconciled items by age rather than by size alone.

#### How do matching rules and write-off analytics change the routine?

Matching rules find an open invoice or bill that fits a transaction and reconcile it. That removes routine work, but it also means a rule can reconcile the wrong item if it is too broad. Review the rules when they are created, and sample automatically reconciled items each month. The release notes also allow an analytic distribution on a write-off created during reconciliation, so small differences such as bank charges can be assigned to a cost centre instead of falling into a general account. Agree which write-offs are acceptable, up to what limit, and who may post them.

#### How does paying bills from Odoo work?

According to the release notes, you can select one or more bills, pay, and confirm with the bank, individually or in batch, through payment initiation (PISP). Availability depends on your bank and country, so check with your bank in Egypt or Saudi Arabia before you plan for it. Where it is available, payment release moves from the bank portal into Odoo, and the bank portal’s own approval chain may no longer be the only gate.

#### What do the red and yellow duplicate warnings mean?

Duplicate detection on invoices and bills has two levels. Red means a highly likely duplicate, to be corrected. Yellow means a potential duplicate, to be investigated before posting. The release notes also describe protection against double payments. Duplicates are one of the most common payables errors we find, so this is useful, but a warning is only a control if someone acts on it and the action is recorded.

#### Which controls need to change?

- Approval before payment: a bill should be approved under your approval matrix before it can be selected for payment, and that approval should be visible on the bill.
- Who can initiate payments: limit payment initiation to a small, named group that does not also create vendors or enter bills.
- Bank-side confirmation: keep the bank’s own authorisation limits aligned with Odoo, so neither side becomes a rubber stamp.
- Duplicate review: no red warning is overridden without a documented reason, and yellow warnings are cleared by someone other than the person who entered the bill.
- Matching rules and write-offs: changes to rules and write-off limits are approved and logged.

> When the payment button moves into the ERP, the approval matrix has to move with it.

#### What should you test before relying on it?

Run the summary report for a period you have already closed and compare it with your own reconciliation. Enter known duplicates and known legitimate repeat bills and check which warning each receives. If payment initiation is offered by your bank, test a batch end to end with real approvals and confirm that a user without payment rights cannot release it. As part of an internal audit, we review the access rights, the rule changes and a sample of payments against approved bills, because the new features are only as strong as the people allowed to use them.

Q: Can I still post manual journal entries to a bank account in Odoo 20?
A: According to the Odoo 20 release notes, all journal entries impacting bank accounts must originate from bank transactions, to prevent manual entries that break bank consistency.

Q: Can I pay vendor bills directly from Odoo 20 in Egypt or Saudi Arabia?
A: Odoo 20 supports paying bills through payment initiation (PISP), individually or in batch, but availability depends on the bank and country. Confirm with your bank first.

Q: What is the difference between red and yellow duplicate warnings?
A: Red marks a highly likely duplicate that should be corrected. Yellow marks a potential duplicate that should be investigated before posting.

### Should you upgrade to Odoo 20? A plan for companies on 17, 18 and 19
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/odoo-20-upgrade-plan-17-18-19/
Published: 2026-10-03

It depends on your current version. On Odoo 17, standard support was planned to end in September 2026, so plan the upgrade now. On 18, upgrade within the next twelve months. On 19, upgrade when a specific Odoo 20 feature pays for itself. Whatever the timing, test the ledger, taxes and e-invoicing before go-live.

- Odoo 17 has reached its planned end of standard support; start planning now.
- Skipping versions in one upgrade request saves time but raises testing risk.
- Tie out the trial balance and open items before and after the upgrade.
- Re-test ETA or ZATCA e-invoicing in a sandbox or pre-production before go-live.

Odoo 20 was released on 24 September 2026, and the first question we hear from finance teams is not about features. It is about timing: do we have to move, and when? The honest answer depends on which version you run today, how much custom code sits on top of it, and whether your e-invoicing integration is stable. This article sets out how we think about the decision and the test plan we use, written for the finance team that will sign off the result.

#### How long is each Odoo version supported?

Odoo supports each major version for three years. According to the Odoo 20 release notes and its published support policy, the planned end of standard support is September 2026 for 17.0, September 2027 for 18.0 and September 2028 for 19.0, which puts Odoo 20 at roughly September 2029. Community and Enterprise share one version number, so the calendar is the same for both, although what is included in each edition is not.

#### What should a company on Odoo 17 do?

Plan the upgrade now. September 2026 has arrived, and running a finance system outside standard support means fixes and upgrade assistance are no longer something you can count on. That does not mean upgrading next week. It means choosing a target version, booking the test window and freezing non-essential customisation so the scope stops moving. For most companies on 17, the target will be Odoo 20 rather than 18 or 19, because it buys the longest support horizon.

#### What about Odoo 18 and Odoo 19?

On 18, aim to upgrade within the next twelve months. Support is planned to run to September 2027, which leaves time for a calm project, but not for an indefinite delay that pushes the work into year-end. On 19, there is no deadline pressure until 2028. Upgrade when a specific Odoo 20 feature pays for itself, for example the inventory valuation changes or the duplicate detection on invoices and bills described in the release notes, and not simply because a new version exists.

#### Can you jump straight from 17 to 20?

On Enterprise, yes. Odoo’s upgrade service can take a database across several versions in one request, for example from 17 to 20. It saves calendar time, but skipping versions raises testing risk: data is transformed through several migration steps at once, and any difference you find is harder to attribute to a single change. If you skip versions, budget more testing, not less. Community databases and custom modules need their own migration route, which is a separate conversation about code.

#### What does a finance-first upgrade test plan cover?

Most upgrade tests check that screens open and buttons work. A finance-first test checks that the numbers did not move. We run the upgrade on a copy of production and test in this order:

- Trial balance tie-out: print the trial balance at the same date before and after, by account, and explain every difference to zero.
- Open items tie-out: compare open receivables, open payables and unreconciled bank lines, by partner and by document, before and after.
- Taxes: confirm every tax, tax grid and fiscal position survived, then rebuild the last filed VAT return from the upgraded database and compare.
- E-invoicing: re-test Egypt’s ETA or Saudi Arabia’s ZATCA integration in the authority’s sandbox or pre-production environment before go-live, including credit notes and rejected documents.
- Custom modules: list every custom module, decide to migrate, replace with standard features or retire, and test each one that touches accounting.
- Access rights: check that roles, approval limits and segregation of duties look the same after the upgrade as they did before it.

Expect some behaviour to change on purpose. According to the Odoo 20 release notes, journal entries that affect bank accounts must now originate from bank transactions, which stops manual entries that break bank consistency. If your team posts bank charges or transfers by manual journal entry today, that habit has to change, and the test should prove the replacement process works.

> An upgrade is finished when the trial balance agrees, not when the login screen loads.

#### Why run a parallel close of one month?

Because a close exercises everything at once: reconciliations, accruals, depreciation, inventory valuation, tax and reporting. We close one recent month in the upgraded test database, following the same month-end close checklist the team uses in production, and compare the financial statements with the ones already approved. Differences found here cost an afternoon. Differences found after go-live cost a restatement.

#### How should cut-over and rollback work?

Pick a cut-over date right after a month is closed and locked, never in the middle of a period. Freeze posting, take a final backup, run the production upgrade, then repeat the trial balance and open items tie-out on the live result before users return. Agree the rollback rule in advance: who decides, by when, and what triggers it. If the tie-out fails and cannot be explained within the agreed window, you restore the backup and try again, rather than fixing the ledger by hand under pressure.

#### Who should own the decision?

The finance lead, with IT and the implementation partner in support. Our Odoo implementation and upgrade team at MFT starts every upgrade with the tie-out templates above, because the people who will defend the numbers to auditors should be the ones who accept them.

Q: Is Odoo 17 still supported after September 2026?
A: Odoo’s planned end of standard support for 17.0 is September 2026. After that date you should not rely on standard support, so companies on 17 should plan their upgrade now.

Q: Can we upgrade from Odoo 17 directly to Odoo 20?
A: On Enterprise, Odoo’s upgrade service can take a database across several versions in one request. Skipping versions raises testing risk, so plan more testing, especially of the ledger, taxes and custom modules.

Q: Do we need to re-test ETA or ZATCA e-invoicing after upgrading?
A: Yes. After any upgrade, re-test the e-invoicing integration in the authority’s sandbox or pre-production environment, including credit notes and rejections, before you go live.

### Odoo 20 inventory valuation changes: what they mean for COGS and margin
URL: https://www.seg-audit.com/en/blog/odoo-20-inventory-valuation-changes/
Published: 2026-10-02

According to the Odoo 20 release notes, valuation accruals can post directly to the inventory valuation account, COGS updates retroactively when a cost changes after delivery, landed costs can target individual products, and inventory can be reported at a past date. Margins become more accurate, so cost changes and period locks need tighter control.

- Retroactive COGS means a late cost change can move margin on goods already delivered.
- Landed costs per product give more precise unit costs on mixed receipts.
- Inventory at a past date and stock aging support month-end and audit work.
- Lock periods, restrict who changes costs, and reconcile stock valuation to the GL monthly.

Inventory is where gross margin is won or lost on paper. The selling price is rarely in dispute; the cost of goods sold behind it often is. Odoo 20 brings a group of changes that sit exactly on that line between inventory and COGS. This article goes through them from a finance point of view, then sets out the controls we would put around them. It assumes you already know the costing methods themselves; if not, start with our guide to FIFO and AVCO valuation in Odoo.

#### What changes in perpetual valuation closing?

According to the Odoo 20 release notes, under perpetual valuation, accrual entries affecting inventory valuation can be made from the inventory valuation closing report, and they post directly to the inventory valuation account rather than through the stock variation account. In practice this shortens the path from a closing adjustment to the balance sheet line it affects. It also means fewer intermediate balances to clear at month end, but only if the team knows the new route and stops reaching for the old one.

#### How does retroactive COGS affect margin?

The release notes describe a retroactive COGS update when a cost changes after delivery. Think of a receipt valued at a provisional cost, goods delivered to a customer, and the final vendor cost arriving later. In earlier versions that difference often stayed in inventory or needed a manual correction. In Odoo 20, cost of goods sold on the delivered quantity follows the corrected cost.

For margin reporting this is better: margin reflects what the goods actually cost. For the close it is a new risk: a cost change made after a month is reported can move COGS for goods that left the warehouse in that month. That is why the period lock matters more, not less, after this change.

#### What is new in landed costs?

Landed costs can now be assigned to individual products of a transfer. When one container holds several products and the freight or customs relates to only some of them, you no longer have to spread the charge across everything received. Unit costs, and therefore margins by product, become more precise. The control question is who decides the allocation and where the supporting document is kept.

#### Which new reports help at month end and in audit?

According to the release notes, Odoo 20 can show inventory at a past date and adds a stock aging report. Inventory at a past date answers the question auditors ask every year: what did you hold at the balance sheet date? Stock aging shows which items have not moved, which is the starting point for a slow-moving or obsolete stock review and any write-down discussion. Neither report decides the write-down for you, but both shorten the evidence work.

#### What else changes for valuation?

- Stock on hand and valuation can be managed without the Inventory app, which suits companies that hold some stock but do not run full warehouse operations.
- Suggested reordering rules propose minimum and maximum quantities from demand history, desired days of coverage and order frequency. They affect how much cash sits in stock, so treat the suggestions as proposals to approve, not settings to accept.
- Intercompany resupply from another company’s warehouse transfers valuation correctly, according to the release notes, which matters for groups that move stock between legal entities.

Feature availability can differ between Community and Enterprise, and much of the accounting automation remains Enterprise-only, so confirm what your edition includes before you design a process around it.

> A more accurate cost is only useful if nobody can change it after the month is reported.

#### Which controls should go around these changes?

Each change above makes valuation more accurate. Each one also gives more people a way to move COGS. We recommend three controls, and we add them to the inventory section of the month-end close checklist:

- Period lock: lock each period once it is reported, so a retroactive cost change cannot silently alter COGS in a closed month. Changes after the lock go through a documented adjustment in the open period.
- Who can change costs: restrict product cost changes, landed cost allocations and valuation accruals to named roles, separate from the people who receive goods, and review a log of cost changes every month.
- Stock valuation to GL reconciliation: at each month end, reconcile the stock valuation report to the inventory valuation account in the general ledger, and explain every difference before the period is locked.

#### Should these changes drive your upgrade?

If inventory is material to your balance sheet and margins are a board-level number, they are a fair reason to plan the move to Odoo 20, especially from an older version. Test them on a copy of your own data first, and compare COGS for a closed month before and after. Where we act as Virtual CFO at MFT, that comparison is the evidence we want before any margin report is trusted.

Q: Does Odoo 20 change COGS on goods already delivered?
A: According to the Odoo 20 release notes, COGS is updated retroactively when a cost changes after delivery. Lock reported periods so such changes do not alter closed months without a documented adjustment.

Q: Can landed costs be assigned to only some products in a receipt?
A: Yes. According to the release notes, Odoo 20 lets you assign landed costs to individual products of a transfer, instead of spreading them across everything received.

Q: How do we confirm inventory valuation is correct at month end?
A: Reconcile the stock valuation report to the inventory valuation account in the general ledger, explain every difference, and only then lock the period. Inventory at a past date helps for prior dates.
